results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Statistics: September 2026 · AI Industry Reviews
highlights:
Renting a data center GPU can cost very different amounts depending on the provider and how the capacity is sold. Teams deciding whether to rent or buy need comparable prices.

Our analysts collected 4,180 GPU-hour rental prices for 14 data center accelerators across 61 cloud providers. We gathered them between March 2 and August 29, 2026. The sample covers the three largest hyperscalers, 22 specialist GPU clouds and the major peer-to-peer marketplaces. We converted every listing to the price of a single GPU-hour so all offers can be compared directly.

In the following sections, we compare H100 prices by provider type, show when owning beats renting, and look at price spreads, trends and commitment discounts.

## H100 Pricing by Provider Category

In the table below, we compare median on-demand rates across three provider categories and express the H100 gap as a premium over the marketplace baseline.

H100 Pricing by Provider Category, September 2026

| Provider Category | H100 | H200 | B200 | H100 Premium |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Marketplace | $2.09 | $3.10 | $4.35 | Baseline |
| Specialist neocloud | $3.28 | $4.28 | $5.95 | +57% |
| Hyperscaler on-demand | $5.64 | $6.72 | $9.10 | +170% |

### Insights

- Hyperscaler H100 on-demand priced at a 170% premium to marketplace in the September sample, or $5.64 versus $2.09 per GPU-hour.
- Specialist neocloud sat between the two at $3.28, a 57% premium to marketplace.
- The same H100 costs far more from a hyperscaler than from a neocloud or a marketplace, so the provider category changes a team's bill as much as the choice of chip does.

The hyperscaler rate buys a support contract, a service level agreement, private networking into an existing cloud footprint, and compliance attestations that most specialist providers do not offer. We sorted providers by those attributes, not by company size, so two of the larger specialist fleets in the sample are in the neocloud row.

## Owning Versus Renting: Break-Even Utilization

In the table below, we model the all-in cost of owning each accelerator per GPU-hour over a five-year life at 85% utilization, then solve for the utilization rate at which ownership matches renting the same card on demand at the sample median.

Owning Versus Renting Break-Even, September 2026

| GPU Model | Street Price (New) | All-In Cost ($/GPU-hr) | Median Rental | Break-Even Utilization |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B200 | $46,500 | $2.68 | $6.05 | 38% |
| NVIDIA H200 | $38,000 | $2.21 | $4.31 | 44% |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM 80GB | $32,500 | $1.92 | $3.24 | 50% |
| NVIDIA A100 80GB | $9,800 | $0.84 | $1.79 | 40% |
| NVIDIA L40S | $8,400 | $0.76 | $1.48 | 44% |
| AMD MI300X | $17,500 | $1.36 | $2.87 | 40% |

### Insights

- An H100 purchase only beats median on-demand rental once the card stays busy at least 50% of the time.
- B200 breaks even at 38% utilization, the lowest threshold in the set, because rental medians remain elevated relative to street price.
- Buying GPUs pays off only for teams that keep them busy, so a company without a steady workload comes out ahead by renting.

## Price Spread by GPU Model

List price for a single provider is a narrow slice of the market. In the table below, we report the sample median on-demand rate for each model plus the 10th and 90th percentile of listings. The spread column is the 90th percentile divided by the 10th, which measures how fragmented pricing is for that card.

GPU Price Spread by Model, September 2026

| GPU Model | Median On-Demand ($/GPU-hr) | 10th Percentile | 90th Percentile | Price Spread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA GB200 (per GPU) | $9.84 | $6.40 | $19.75 | 3.1x |
| NVIDIA B300 | $8.12 | $5.15 | $14.60 | 2.8x |
| NVIDIA B200 | $6.05 | $3.42 | $11.80 | 3.4x |
| NVIDIA H200 | $4.31 | $2.58 | $9.45 | 3.7x |
| NVIDIA H100 80GB | $3.24 | $1.44 | $8.90 | 6.2x |
| NVIDIA A100 80GB | $1.79 | $0.92 | $5.15 | 5.6x |
| NVIDIA L40S | $1.48 | $0.74 | $3.60 | 4.9x |
| NVIDIA V100 | $1.51 | $0.68 | $2.90 | 4.3x |
| NVIDIA RTX 5090 | $0.58 | $0.29 | $1.35 | 4.7x |
| NVIDIA RTX 4090 | $0.41 | $0.21 | $0.98 | 4.7x |
| AMD MI300X | $2.87 | $1.72 | $5.90 | 3.4x |
| Google TPU v6e (per chip) | $2.58 | $1.18 | $3.10 | 2.6x |

### Insights

- H100 showed the widest spread in the sample at 6.2x, because it is sold both as premium enterprise capacity and as surplus capacity.
- V100 rented above the newer L40S in half of the markets sampled, which matches demand from buyers whose software is pinned to older CUDA versions.
- Prices for the same chip vary widely, so comparing several providers pays off. MI300X rented for 33% less than H200, which gives buyers who can run on AMD hardware another way to cut cost.

## H100 Prices by Provider Channel, Q3 2023 to Q3 2026

In the table below, we show the median quarterly on-demand H100 rate in each of the three provider channels.

H100 Prices by Provider Channel, Q3 2023 to Q3 2026

| Quarter | Hyperscaler | Specialist Neocloud | Marketplace |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q3 2023 | $8.05 | $4.60 | $3.85 |
| Q4 2023 | $7.72 | $4.12 | $3.40 |
| Q1 2024 | $7.94 | $3.62 | $2.92 |
| Q2 2024 | $8.60 | $3.10 | $2.66 |
| Q3 2024 | $9.18 | $2.94 | $2.51 |
| Q4 2024 | $8.85 | $3.28 | $2.38 |
| Q1 2025 | $8.64 | $3.44 | $2.24 |
| Q2 2025 | $7.02 | $3.31 | $2.05 |
| Q3 2025 | $6.38 | $3.36 | $1.98 |
| Q4 2025 | $6.15 | $3.18 | $1.92 |
| Q1 2026 | $5.70 | $3.02 | $2.11 |
| Q2 2026 | $5.92 | $3.35 | $2.24 |
| Q3 2026 | $5.64 | $3.28 | $2.09 |

H100 rental prices by provider channel

In the quarterly series above, hyperscaler pricing rose through 2024 while reserved enterprise capacity stayed scarce, then fell in mid-2025 as specialist competition forced Hopper fleets to reprice. Marketplace rates fell about 50% from the third quarter of 2023 to the fourth quarter of 2025 as resellers and colocation tenants listed idle cards. We read the 2026 uptick across all three channels as the first sustained reversal in that series, and we tie it to high-bandwidth memory costs passing into rental rates.

## Commitment Discounts Versus On-Demand

In the table below, we quantify the median discount each commitment structure earns against the same provider's on-demand rate, plus the effective hourly rate a three-year commitment produces.

GPU Commitment Discounts, September 2026

| GPU Model | Spot Discount | 1-Year Reserved | 3-Year Reserved | Effective 3-Year Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B200 | -31% | -21% | -39% | $3.69 |
| NVIDIA H200 | -38% | -24% | -42% | $2.50 |
| NVIDIA H100 80GB | -44% | -27% | -46% | $1.75 |
| NVIDIA A100 80GB | -57% | -31% | -49% | $0.91 |
| NVIDIA L40S | -63% | -34% | -51% | $0.73 |

### Insights

- Spot discounts widened with hardware age, from 31% on B200 to 63% on L40S.
- One-year reserved discounts stayed smaller than spot discounts on every model priced, so they are the weakest value for interruptible work.
- A three-year H100 commitment now prices below the median marketplace on-demand rate, a first in this series, so a team with predictable demand saves the most by committing.

...

Renting AI chips has become much cheaper for older models, while the newest chips still cost a lot because supply is short. Where a team rents and how long it commits for each change the bill by a large amount.

Buying hardware outright only pays off for teams that keep it busy most of the time, so most teams are better off renting until their workload is steady.

So if you rent GPUs, match the contract to your workload: commit long only for steady jobs, and use marketplaces or spot capacity for everything else.

results.title: DigitalOcean GPU Droplets: What They Cost and What They Lose
highlights:
> TL;DR: GPU Droplets are billed per second and priced per GPU: $4.41/hr for an H100, $4.47 for an H200, $2.59 for an MI300X, $1.57 for an L40S or RTX 6000 Ada, $0.76 for an RTX 4000 Ada, as of DigitalOcean's August 1, 2026 pricing. Against 1,044 live offers from nine providers, that is roughly double the market low on the small cards and about a third above the H100 median, but it is genuinely competitive on H200, where the market median is $4.59. The thing to actually plan around is storage: the 5 TiB "scratch" disk attached to every multi-GPU config is documented as non-persistent, is excluded from snapshots, and is lost when the Droplet is destroyed, and destroying is the only way to stop the meter, because a powered-off GPU Droplet keeps billing in full.

...

| GPU | VRAM | Count | vCPU | RAM | Boot disk | Scratch disk | Per GPU/hr |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA HGX H200 | 141 GB | 1 or 8 | 24 | 240 GiB | 720 GiB NVMe | 5 TiB NVMe | $4.47 |
| NVIDIA HGX H100 | 80 GB | 1 or 8 | 20 | 240 GiB | 720 GiB NVMe | 5 TiB NVMe | $4.41 |
| AMD Instinct MI325X | 256 GB | 1 or 8 | 20 | 164 GiB | 720 GiB NVMe | 5 TiB NVMe | $3.80 |
| AMD Instinct MI300X | 192 GB | 1 or 8 | 20 | 240 GiB | 720 GiB NVMe | 5 TiB NVMe | $2.59 |
| NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada | 48 GB | 1 | 8 | 64 GiB | 500 GiB NVMe | N/A | $1.57 |
| NVIDIA L40S | 48 GB | 1 | 8 | 64 GiB | 500 GiB NVMe | N/A | $1.57 |
| NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada | 20 GB | 1 | 8 | 32 GiB | 500 GiB NVMe | N/A | $0.76 |

Two details worth pulling out of that table before the price comparison. The multi-GPU shapes are sold as 1 or 8. There is no 2, 4, or 6. And DigitalOcean's own two sources disagree on the billing floor: the pricing page says GPU Droplets are "billed per second with a 5-minute minimum billing period", while the Droplet pricing documentation says they are "billed per second with a minimum charge of 60 seconds or $0.01, whichever is higher". Both are DigitalOcean's; we have not been able to reconcile them, and on a workload of short bursty runs the difference is real, so budget for the five-minute floor.

...

We run a marketplace across providers, so we can price the same card in a lot of places at once. The figures below come from our public GPU price index, generated 2026-08-28 from 1,044 live offers across nine providers and 126 regions. Every number is a per-GPU hourly rate. No row is a whole-node price divided by nothing, which is the single most common way these comparisons go wrong.

| GPU | DigitalOcean | Market low | Market median | Offers / providers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 80GB | $4.41 | $2.20 | $3.29 | 81 / 6 |
| H200 141GB | $4.47 | $3.93 | $4.59 | 45 / 4 |
| MI300X 192GB | $2.59 | $2.39 | $2.39 | 7 / 2 |
| L40S 48GB | $1.57 | $0.79 | $0.99 | 39 / 3 |
| RTX 6000 Ada 48GB | $1.57 | $0.66 | $0.74 | 14 / 3 |
| RTX 4000 Ada 20GB | $0.76 | $0.28 | $0.28 | 5 / 2 |

Read that honestly and it splits in three.

On the small cards, DigitalOcean is roughly double the market. An RTX 4000 Ada at $0.76 against a $0.28 low is a 2.7x spread; RTX 6000 Ada at $1.57 against $0.66 is 2.4x. If your workload is a single 20-48GB card doing inference or fine-tuning, this is the most expensive way to buy it that still counts as a fair price.

...

Worth keeping in mind on all of the above: this is a snapshot, not a floor. H100-class pricing has actually been climbing market-wide since mid-2025 after two years of decline, for reasons that have nothing to do with any single vendor. See why cloud GPU prices are rising again in 2026 for the supply-side story.

...

The boot disk (720 GiB on the 8x shapes, 500 GiB on the single cards) is the persistent one: OS, frameworks, and anything you meant to keep. The 5 TiB NVMe scratch disk beside it is not. DigitalOcean's documentation is direct about this. It is "a local, non-persistent disk to store data for staging purposes, like inference and training". "The scratch disk is not included in snapshots of the Droplet." "If you destroy or recreate a GPU Droplet, the scratch disk is lost." "The scratch disk has no redundancy, so hardware failures may also lead to loss of data." And it is "not automatically mounted": you get a pre-formatted ext4 partition and you mount it yourself (DigitalOcean docs).

...

DigitalOcean's billing documentation states it plainly: "You are still billed for GPU Droplets that are powered off. The GPU and other compute resources stay reserved on the hypervisor even when the Droplet is not running." And then the remedy: "To end billing, destroy the GPU Droplet."

Put the two facts side by side and the trap is structural rather than sneaky.

...

The arithmetic is not small. An 8x H100 GPU Droplet is 8 x $4.41 = $35.28/hr. Leave it powered off across a weekend you were not working (48 hours), and that is $1,693.44 for an idle machine. Leave a single H200 powered off for a week and it is $751. Powering off buys you nothing but the illusion of thrift.

results.title: Neoclod GPU Prices Surge 25% in Q2, Data Center ROI Period Shrinks to 2 Years | Gate News
highlights:
According to Korea Investment & Securities analysts on August 1, neoclod companies reported significant GPU rental fee increases in Q2 results. CoreWeave implemented a 25% price increase across all products in July, while Nebius saw capacity auction prices 15% higher than previous highs. IREN's three-year contract rates jumped 125% versus November 2025, with five-year rates up 70%. Consequentially, data center investment payback periods have compressed from the traditional 4-5 years to under 2 years, with Nebius noting that $20 million per megawatt (MW) contracts now enable sub-two-year ROI, and IREN citing recent $25 million per MW agreements in negotiation.

Analysts attribute the surge to accelerating token consumption by enterprises. Google disclosed in Q2 that over 500 companies now consume 1 trillion-plus tokens, with 2,000+ consuming 100 billion tokens. Microsoft reported a 400% year-over-year increase in customers reaching annual token consumption of 1 trillion, driving higher profitability for AI model developers and intensifying data center pricing pressure.

results.title: Neocloud Companies Cut Data Center Payback to 2 Years With GPU Price Hikes | Gate News
highlights:
Key Takeaways

- CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN raised GPU prices significantly during Q2, with CoreWeave implementing 25% increases.
- Data center investment payback periods fell from 4-5 years to approximately 2 years due to price increases.
- Google reported over 500 companies consuming more than 1 trillion tokens during Q2 conference call.

Global neocloud companies emphasized GPU pricing increases during Q2 earnings announcements, with data center investment payback periods shortening from the previous 4-5 years to around 2 years, according to analysis by Korea Investment & Securities. The pricing surge stems from rapid growth in enterprise token consumption, suggesting similar changes may eventually affect Korean data center operators. Neocloud refers to service providers offering GPU-based cloud computing specialized for artificial intelligence model training and inference.

## CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN Announce GPU Pricing Increases

Korea Investment & Securities researchers Jung Ho-yoon and Hwang In-jun stated in a report that neocloud companies uniformly emphasized GPU pricing increases during Q2 conference calls. CoreWeave, the leading neocloud company, implemented a 25% price increase across all products in July. Nebius announced that capacity sold at its Q2 auction achieved prices 15% higher than the previous peak. IREN reported that 3-year contract unit prices increased 125% compared to last November, while 5-year contract prices rose 70%.

## Data Center Payback Periods Drop to Under 2 Years

The price increases are directly improving profitability metrics. Nebius stated that investment payback would take less than 2 years at prices exceeding $20 million per megawatt. IREN disclosed signing a 3-year contract at $20 million per MW, with recent contract discussions reaching $25 million per MW. The researchers noted that the data center industry, which previously required 4-5 years for investment recovery based on 5-year contracts, has reached a level where investment payback is achievable through 3-year contracts due to unit price increases.

## Google and Microsoft Report Surge in Enterprise Token Consumption

Major neocloud companies cited increased inference demand as the reason for pricing increases. During its Q2 conference call, Google reported over 500 companies consuming more than 1 trillion tokens and over 2,000 companies consuming more than 100 billion tokens. Microsoft announced that the number of customers reaching 1 trillion annual token consumption increased 400% year-over-year. Model developers like Anthropic and OpenAI charge enterprise customers based on token usage, while GPU costs are tied to hourly rates or fixed contracts, creating a structure where revenue grows as enterprise token usage increases.

...

The researchers suggested attention should be paid to the Korean data center industry. They explained that because data center cost structures consist mostly of fixed expenses such as rent, electricity, depreciation, and principal/interest payments, price increases can lead to rapid profitability improvements. The researchers stated that while Korean and US situations are not identical, if the root cause of these changes is increased enterprise token consumption, similar changes may be observed in Korea over the long term. They identified Naver, Samsung SDS, and NHN as noteworthy companies.

results.title: A consumer GPU moved 21% in a day. | Damon Perry
highlights:
A consumer GPU moved 21% in a day.

Checked my QLABS Terminal™ just now: an RTX 4070S on Vast.ai jumped +21.3% in the last 24 hours.

That's not a typo — that's what happens when GPU rental is a real spot market, not a fixed-price product. Prices move because supply and demand actually move.

Same story with the enterprise chips, just slower. An NVIDIA H200 SXM rents for $2.29/hr on Lambda Labs' spot listings right now, and Azure's own published on-demand rate for the same chip is $5.54/hr — same hardware, over 2x apart, today.

This is exactly why I'm building the QLABS Terminal™: a live price tape for compute, the same way any other commodity market has one. It pulls pricing across 11 providers — hyperscalers, neoclouds, decentralized marketplaces — clearly labeled as live feed vs. published reference, never blended into one fake number. Right now it's tracking 7,193 GPUs in real time.

results.title: Spent a few hours recently with family friends who've just entered the GPU-as-a-service market. Naturally, I drew the parallel to cloud economics - years of AWS and GCP bills across two ventures … | Vaibhav Anand
highlights:
On raw H100 pricing, hyperscalers aren't cheaper - they're 2.5x to 5x more expensive than neoclouds, at every tier I checked:

→ On-demand: AWS ~$6.88/GPU-hr, Azure ~$12.29/GPU-hr, vs. ~$2.39/GPU-hr on GPU-first providers like RunPod → 3-year reserved: AWS's deepest commitment tier (~$3.10/GPU-hr) closes a lot of the gap - enough to beat most neocloud on-demand rates but neocloud reserved contracts (~$1.84/GPU-hr) still undercut it

The gap compresses with commitment. It doesn't invert.

India adds a sharper version of the same pattern. Commercial hyperscaler H100 access here runs roughly ₹210–335/GPU-hr. IndiaAI Mission-empanelled providers (Yotta, E2E Networks, Tata Communications, CtrlS) price at ₹115–150/GPU-hr before subsidy which is already below hyperscaler rates and the mission's 40% compute subsidy pushes effective rates for approved projects to ₹65–116/GPU-hr.

So why did I expect the opposite? Because in my own ventures, the premium I paid AWS and GCP wasn't for compute - it was for the platform: managed services, Data Localization, compliance certs, and not having to think about infrastructure so the team could focus on product. That's a real and often correct trade. But it's a different question from "who's cheaper per GPU-hour," and conflating the two is an easy trap especially when comparing hyperscaler reserved pricing against neocloud on-demand pricing, which flatters the hyperscaler side.

For India's emerging GPU-as-a-service providers, the IndiaAI subsidy isn't just a startup discount. It's underwriting a pricing floor that private capital would take years to reach on its own and it changes who gets to experiment with compute-heavy AI in the first place.

The real question for any founder evaluating this isn't "which is cheaper" it's "does my workload need the hyperscaler bundle, or just the GPU." Most early-stage AI teams need the GPU.

results.title: JPMorgan: Pengeluaran token AI naik 7% pada Agustus, biaya sewa GPU B200 turun 1,5%, harga spot DRAM naik selama lima bulan berturut-turut | Berita Gate | Gate News
highlights: Menurut laporan JPMorgan pada 28 Agustus, belanja token AI di OpenRouter pada Agustus meningkat 7% dibandingkan bulan sebelumnya dan melonjak 12 kali lipat secara tahunan. Volume token meningkat 47% dibandingkan bulan sebelumnya dan 28 kali lipat secara tahunan, dengan model berbiaya rendah seperti GPT-5.6 Luna menyumbang 99% dari pertumbuhan tambahan tersebut. Sementara itu, tarif sewa GPU B200 turun 1,5% menjadi 5,63 dolar AS per jam, menandai penurunan bulanan pertama sejak indeks tersebut diluncurkan pada September 2025. Harga spot DRAM melanjutkan reli selama lima bulan, dengan DDR5 16Gb mencapai 50,20 dolar AS (+6% dibandingkan bulan sebelumnya, +880% secara tahunan), sementara NAND mengakhiri penurunan selama empat bulan di level 30,50 dolar AS per terabit (+14% dibandingkan bulan sebelumnya, +470% secara tahunan).

results.title: JPMorgan: el gasto en tokens de IA aumenta un 7 % en agosto, el alquiler de GPU B200 cae un 1,5 % y los precios spot de DRAM suben por quinto mes consecutivo | Gate News
highlights: Según el informe de JPMorgan del 28 de agosto, el gasto en tokens de OpenRouter AI aumentó un 7% intermensual en agosto, mientras que se multiplicó por 12 interanualmente. El volumen de tokens creció un 47% intermensual y se multiplicó por 28 interanualmente, y los modelos de bajo coste, como GPT-5.6 Luna, representaron el 99% del crecimiento adicional. Mientras tanto, las tarifas de alquiler de GPU B200 descendieron un 1,5%, hasta los 5,63 dólares por hora, lo que marcó la primera caída mensual desde el lanzamiento del índice en septiembre de 2025. Los precios spot de la DRAM mantuvieron un repunte de cinco meses, con los chips DDR5 de 16 Gb alcanzando los 50,20 dólares (+6% intermensual, +880% interanual), mientras que la NAND puso fin a un descenso de cuatro meses y alcanzó los 30,50 dólares por terabit (+14% intermensual, +470% interanual).

results.title: NVIDIA AI Factory Compute Is Becoming an Investable Asset Class - Future Tech Markets
highlights:
The market is also demonstrating the durability of NVIDIA compute economics. One-year H100 rental pricing rose from about $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to about $2.35 per GPU-hour in March 2026. Cross-provider on-demand median pricing rose from roughly $2.00 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.70 in June 2026. Blackwell capacity commands a premium, with reported B200 cloud rates spanning approximately $5.30 to $7.05 per GPU-hour.

That is what makes NVIDIA AI factories different. Their value is not fixed at installation: CUDA continuously improves their output; the installed base remains productive well beyond its initial depreciation period; and the same standard architecture serves a deep, growing global market of AI workloads.
